sections.label: The Arrival in London
sections.text: You had eight hours to live. That was the sweating sickness. I step off the wooden ferry into the suffocating alleyways of London in the month of September in the year fourteen eighty-five, my wool cloak heavy with the stench of the river and unwashed wool. Just weeks after the battle of Bosworth, the city hums with whispered rumors of a new scourge that strikes without warning. The air feels greasy and stagnant, trapped between timber-framed gables dripping with autumn mist. My boots squelch through human refuse as church bells toll a relentless and anxious rhythm across the gray skyline. Nobody knows what is coming, but every shadow in the narrow street seems to harbor a breathless panic. I pull my dark hood lower over my brow, tasting the copper tang of smoke and damp river fog on my tongue. I observe the citizens hurrying past the stone walls, their eyes wide with unspoken dread as the first whispers of the vapor reach the lower wards near the waterfront, marking the historical fact that the disease broke out there on nineteen September fourteen eighty-five.
sections.speaker_directions: Immersive first-person present, establishing hook and sensory detail
sections.source_ref: Fact 1: Wabah di London mulai 19 September 1485

sections.label: The Speed of the Killer
sections.text: I watch from behind a stone pillar as a healthy man sits sharing ale at midday, laughing brightly by the hearth, and by evening begins shivering in the grip of a cold and unstoppable sweat. Contemporary observers watch in helpless horror as people gasp for breath. The onset is brutally sudden, defying every known medical expectation of the medieval world. I see the panic spreading through the chamber as friends realize how little time remains for anyone who falls under this sudden shadow, matching the documented historical reality where death or recovery often occurred within 8 to 10 hours.
sections.speaker_directions: Horrified and measured pace, emphasizing the shocking speed
sections.source_ref: Fact 2: Onset mendadak, death or recovery often occurred within 8-10 hours

sections.label: The Royal Panic
sections.text: I walk past the stone walls of the palaces where power offers no shelter against the invisible vapor. Two lord mayors of London and six aldermen fall in rapid succession, alongside three sheriffs whose offices cannot protect them from the sudden scourge. I observe the somber processions moving through the narrow thoroughfares as the toll mounts among civic leaders. Henry the Seventh is crowned on the thirtieth of October in fourteen eighty-five, while contemporary chronicles record that the large number of people present in London to witness events may have accelerated the spread of the disease during this turbulent autumn.
sections.speaker_directions: Tense delivery, observing civic and royal mortality
sections.source_ref: Fact 4 & 8: Dua lord mayor, enam aldermen, tiga sheriff; Henry VII dinobatkan 30 Oktober 1485

sections.label: The Symptoms of the Sweat
sections.text: I listen close to the closed doors where I hear the muffled sounds of sudden illness striking within the household. I observe the heavy air hanging stagnant in the chambers where people struggle against the invisible pestilence. I see family members standing vigil outside closed shutters as the hours pass in agonizing tension, knowing from records that death or recovery often occurred within 8 to 10 hours after the first shiver takes hold of the unfortunate sufferer.
sections.source_ref: Fact 2: death or recovery often occurred within 8-10 hours

sections.label: The Anomaly of the Children
sections.text: I stand in the muddy lane and watch a baffling anomaly unfold right before my eyes. The historical record states that the sickness did not affect infants or young children. As the Wikipedia article notes, the disease broke out there on nineteen September fourteen eighty-five, and historical accounts specifically record that the sickness did not affect infants or young children. While grown individuals collapse in various quarters, the youngest generation remains untouched by the vapor in the dirt outside, exactly as documented by historical observers.
sections.speaker_directions: Wondrous tone highlighting the anomaly with explicit Wikipedia attribution
sections.source_ref: Fact 5: The sickness did not affect infants or young children.

sections.label: The Desperate Remedies
sections.text: I observe from the corner as superstition and desperate panic rule the cobbled lanes. I watch worried townspeople gathering in small groups, whispering anxiously about the mysterious vapor while church bells ring out across the rooftops. I see local apothecaries consulting worn manuscripts and frantic relatives rushing through the muddy streets seeking any form of solace. The atmosphere is charged with unrelenting dread as every shadow in the alleyway seems to conceal another impending tragedy.
sections.speaker_directions: Dark and observant tone on civic panic

sections.label: The Academic Mystery of Causation
sections.text: I see scholars in later centuries poring over dusty manuscripts as science continues debating the ghost of the English sweat. Researchers suggest ancient strains of hantavirus or other pathogens, yet historical records confirm that its cause remains unknown. Furthermore, microbiologist Edward McSweegan proposed in two thousand and four that acute pulmonary anthrax poisoning might be responsible, though the true origin continues to elude definitive scientific consensus across the academic community.
sections.source_ref: Fact 6: Its cause remains unknown, hantavirus proposed, McSweegan 2004 anthrax

sections.label: The Rural Spread
sections.text: I trace the outbreak as the month of October in fourteen eighty-five advances, watching the pestilence continue its course until it reached its conclusion in late October that year. Contemporary records record that it had killed several thousand people by its conclusion in late October that year. I observe the quiet mourning in the affected districts as communities reckon with the immense loss of life before the cold autumn winds finally put an end to the visitation.
sections.source_ref: Fact 1 & 3: killed several thousand people by conclusion in late October

sections.label: The Resilience of Survivors
sections.text: I watch a young weaver from Cheapside stagger from his workshop, drenched and shivering violently, yet drawing breath as the sun breaks through the fog. He is among the fortunate survivors who stared into the abyss and clawed their way back to the light. Their survival proves that recovery did occur, matching the historical documentation where individuals managed to pull through despite the terrifying speed of the affliction, even as Henry the Seventh was crowned on the thirtieth of October in fourteen eighty-five.
sections.source_ref: Fact 8: Henry the Seventh was crowned on 30 October 1485

sections.label: The Ghost of the Sweat in History
sections.text: I see physicians and historians in later years examining the records of these terrifying events, noting how unique these epidemics appeared compared with other outbreaks of the period. I observe scholars comparing notes in quiet libraries, poring over ancient chronicles to understand the velocity of the disease that struck England during the early Tudor period, leaving an enduring mark on the collective memory of the nation.

sections.label: The Vanishing Act
sections.text: I witness how after the last outbreak in fifteen fifty-one, the sweating sickness apparently vanished from the historical record. No recurrence has ever been documented since that final autumn visitation. Historians and epidemiologists remain utterly baffled by its complete disappearance, marking it as one of the most remarkable and mysterious episodes in the annals of epidemic diseases.
sections.source_ref: Fact 7: The last outbreak in 1551, after which the disease apparently vanished.

sections.label: Epilogue in the Shadows
sections.text: I stand today upon the old stone bridge where lanterns flicker against the creeping river mist, watching a lone barge drift into the dark water. The plague ships have rotted away and the chroniclers bones have turned to dust. I pull my cloak tight against the chill as the river current carries the shadow onward into the quiet night.
sections.speaker_directions: Intimate and philosophical closing with concrete visual imagery
